questions.stem: How many leads must show ST elevation before you can call a STEMI?
questions.why: Two or more contiguous leads — leads looking at the same wall — is the threshold. A single lead is not enough, because one electrode can lie or drift.

options.t: All twelve leads, to rule out pericarditis
options.why: Diffuse elevation across all leads argues for pericarditis rather than a STEMI.

options.t: Any single lead, if the elevation exceeds 2 mm
options.why: Elevation in one isolated lead is far more likely to be artifact or a normal variant.

options.t: Four or more leads, spread across two walls
options.why: Four leads would mean a very large infarct; two contiguous leads meet the threshold.

options.t: Two or more contiguous leads

questions.stem: What counts as significant ST elevation in the limb leads?
questions.why: One millimetre of elevation at the J point in two contiguous limb leads is the usual threshold. V2 and V3 need more — roughly 2 mm in men and 1.5 mm in women — because they are normally elevated slightly.

options.t: 5 mm, one large box
options.why: One large box of elevation is a very large finding and well above the threshold.

options.t: 2 mm in every lead regardless of location
options.why: 2 mm applies to certain precordial leads, not uniformly.

options.t: 1 mm, or one small box
0.5 mm, half a small box
options.why: Half a box is within normal variation and measurement error.

questions.stem: ST elevation appears in V3 and V4. Which artery and wall does that point to?
questions.why: V3 and V4 face the anterior wall, fed by the LAD. That is the vessel behind the widow-maker's reputation — it supplies a large share of the left ventricle.

options.t: The circumflex, lateral wall
options.why: The lateral wall shows in V5, V6, I and aVL.

options.t: The left anterior descending, anterior wall
The right coronary artery, inferior wall
options.why: The inferior wall shows in II, III and aVF.

options.t: The posterior descending artery, posterior wall
options.why: Posterior involvement shows as reciprocal depression in V1 through V3, or elevation in V7 through V9.

questions.stem: You see ST elevation in II, III and aVF. What extra lead should you obtain, and why?
questions.why: An inferior STEMI is usually an RCA lesion, and the RCA also supplies the right ventricle proximally. V4R identifies that involvement — which matters because those patients are preload-dependent and nitroglycerin can drop their pressure sharply.

options.t: V7 through V9, to check the posterior wall
options.why: Posterior leads are worth adding when V1–V3 show reciprocal depression, not routinely with every inferior MI.

options.t: V4R, to check for right ventricular involvement
A second lead II, to confirm the elevation is real
options.why: The elevation is already present in three contiguous leads.

options.t: A repeat V1 and V2, to confirm septal sparing
options.why: Repeating a lead confirms placement but does not add a view.

questions.stem: What do reciprocal ST depressions add to a 12-lead reading?
questions.why: Leads on the opposite side of the heart see the same injury current going away from them, producing depression. Their presence strongly raises confidence that the elevation is a real occlusion.

options.t: They make a true infarct much more likely
They identify a second, separate area of infarction
options.why: Reciprocal change is the same injury viewed from the opposite side, not another infarct.

options.t: They indicate the infarct has begun to resolve
options.why: Reciprocal change appears with the injury, not as it resolves.

options.t: They mean the elevation should be disregarded as artifact
options.why: Reciprocal change supports the finding rather than undermining it.

questions.stem: An inferior STEMI is showing reciprocal changes. Where should you look for them?
questions.why: Inferior and high lateral are opposite each other, so inferior elevation is mirrored by depression in I and aVL. Anterior elevation mirrors into II, III and aVF.

options.t: V5 and V6
options.why: The low lateral leads sit closer to the inferior wall and do not reliably show reciprocal change here.

options.t: II and III
options.why: Those are the leads showing the elevation itself.

options.t: V1 and V2
options.why: Depression in V1 and V2 raises the question of posterior involvement instead.

options.t: I and aVL

questions.stem: V1 through V3 show ST depression with tall R waves. What should that suggest?
questions.why: No standard lead looks directly at the posterior wall, so a posterior infarct appears reversed in V1–V3: depression instead of elevation, and tall R waves instead of Q waves. V7 through V9 confirm it.

options.t: Left ventricular hypertrophy
options.why: Hypertrophy produces tall R waves in the lateral leads with strain, not this pattern.

options.t: Anterior ischemia without infarction
options.why: Anterior ischemia would not produce the tall R waves seen here.

options.t: A posterior infarct seen in mirror image
A normal variant in a young athletic patient
options.why: Depression with tall anterior R waves is not a normal variant.

questions.stem: What is the earliest 12-lead change in an evolving infarct, often preceding ST elevation?
questions.why: The sequence is hyperacute T waves, then ST elevation, then T wave inversion, then pathologic Q waves. Catching the hyperacute phase means catching the infarct early.

options.t: Pathologic Q waves in the affected leads
options.why: Q waves appear hours to days later and mark completed necrosis.

options.t: Tall, peaked hyperacute T waves
T wave inversion in the affected leads
options.why: Inversion generally follows the elevation rather than preceding it.

options.t: A widened QRS in the affected leads
options.why: QRS widening reflects conduction disease rather than early ischemia.

questions.stem: What does a pathologic Q wave tell you?
questions.why: A Q wave deeper than a third of the R or wider than 0.04 seconds means an electrically silent window — necrotic muscle that no longer depolarizes. It is a scar, and it stays.

options.t: The infarct is actively evolving right now
options.why: Active injury shows as ST elevation; the Q wave marks what is already done.

options.t: Tissue in that region is dead and no longer conducts
The vessel has reperfused and function is returning
options.why: Reperfusion is judged by resolving ST segments, not by Q waves.

options.t: The patient is a candidate for immediate thrombolytics
options.why: Established necrosis is what thrombolytics can no longer reverse.

questions.stem: How do you tell a right from a left bundle branch block on a 12-lead?
questions.why: With a QRS at or over 0.12, look at V1. A terminal upward deflection — the classic rabbit ears — is a right bundle branch block; a broad downward one is a left. The turn-signal mnemonic: up is right, down is left.

options.t: Look at V1: up is right, down is left
Measure the PR interval — right blocks lengthen it
options.why: PR length reflects AV nodal conduction, above the bundle branches.

options.t: Look at lead II for an upright or inverted P wave
options.why: The P wave reports atrial origin, not ventricular conduction.

options.t: Compare aVR and aVL for opposing deflections
options.why: Those two leads do not separate the bundle branch blocks.

questions.stem: Why does a new left bundle branch block matter in a patient with chest pain?
questions.why: A left bundle branch block distorts ST segments and T waves on its own, so ordinary STEMI criteria stop working. A new one with ischemic symptoms is treated as a STEMI equivalent.

options.t: It requires immediate transcutaneous pacing
options.why: A stable patient with a bundle branch block does not need pacing.

options.t: It rules out an infarct as the cause of the pain
options.why: A new block in this setting raises suspicion rather than lowering it.

options.t: It slows the ventricular rate to a dangerous degree
options.why: A bundle branch block changes conduction pathway, not rate.

options.t: It can conceal the ST changes of an acute infarct

questions.stem: A 12-lead shows ST elevation in nearly every lead with PR depression. What does that suggest?
questions.why: Pericarditis inflames the whole sac, so elevation is diffuse rather than territorial, it is usually concave upward, and PR depression is characteristic. Reciprocal changes are absent, which is the key difference from a STEMI.

options.t: Hyperkalemia with peaked T waves
options.why: Hyperkalemia peaks T waves and widens the QRS without diffuse ST elevation.

options.t: A very large anterior STEMI
options.why: An infarct follows one vessel's territory rather than appearing everywhere at once.

options.t: Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain
options.why: Hypertrophy produces high voltage with strain, not diffuse elevation with PR depression.

options.t: Pericarditis

questions.stem: Which finding argues that ST elevation is benign early repolarization rather than infarction?
questions.why: Early repolarization is a common benign variant, especially in young men: concave elevation, a notched J point, and no reciprocal changes. Serial 12-leads are what settle a genuinely ambiguous tracing.

options.t: Elevation that increases across serial tracings
options.why: Elevation that evolves over time is the pattern of an active infarct.

options.t: Concave elevation with a notched J point
Convex, dome-shaped elevation across contiguous leads
options.why: That convex morphology is the worrying one.

options.t: Reciprocal depression in the opposite leads
options.why: Reciprocal change points strongly toward a true occlusion.

questions.stem: A patient with ongoing chest pain has a normal first 12-lead. What should you do?
questions.why: The first tracing is a snapshot of one moment in an evolving process. Repeat it every 5 to 10 minutes with ongoing symptoms, and after any change in the patient's condition.

options.t: Withhold aspirin and nitroglycerin until changes appear
options.why: Aspirin and nitroglycerin are given on the clinical picture, not on the tracing alone.

options.t: Treat the pain as non-cardiac and downgrade priority
options.why: A normal tracing does not rule out an ACS.

options.t: Repeat it — one normal tracing excludes nothing
Cancel the STEMI alert but keep the patient monitored
options.why: There would not be an alert to cancel if the first tracing was normal.

questions.stem: What single field action most improves outcome in a confirmed STEMI?
questions.why: The whole point of a prehospital 12-lead is time. Transmitting it or calling the alert early is what lets the receiving hospital assemble the team before the patient arrives — every minute of ischemia costs myocardium.

options.t: Obtaining a full set of vitals in both arms
options.why: Bilateral pressures are useful for a suspected dissection, not for reperfusion time.

options.t: Establishing two large-bore IVs before transport
options.why: Access matters, but it does not shorten the time to reperfusion.

options.t: Early notification so the cath lab can activate
Giving three nitroglycerin doses before departing the scene
options.why: Nitroglycerin manages symptoms; it does not open the vessel.

questions.stem: Why is nitroglycerin used cautiously in a right ventricular infarct?
questions.why: A right ventricle that has infarcted cannot generate its own force, so it depends on volume to push blood through to the left side. Nitroglycerin pools blood in the veins and removes that volume, and the pressure can fall hard.

options.t: It has no effect on the coronary arteries of the right side
options.why: Nitroglycerin dilates coronary vessels generally; the problem is its venous effect.

options.t: That ventricle depends on the preload it removes
It raises myocardial oxygen demand in an ischemic ventricle
options.why: Nitroglycerin lowers demand by reducing preload and afterload.

options.t: It reliably triggers reflex tachycardia in these patients
options.why: Some reflex tachycardia can occur, but the hazard here is the drop in filling pressure.

questions.stem: Which contraindication to nitroglycerin is easiest to miss and most dangerous?
questions.why: Sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and similar drugs plus nitroglycerin can produce profound, refractory hypotension. Patients do not always volunteer it, so it has to be asked directly.

options.t: Chest pain that has lasted longer than an hour
options.why: Duration does not contraindicate nitroglycerin.

options.t: A systolic pressure of 140
options.why: That pressure is well above the threshold that would rule nitroglycerin out.

options.t: A history of hypertension on medication
options.why: Treated hypertension is not itself a contraindication.

options.t: A PDE-5 inhibitor taken in the last 24 hours

questions.stem: Why should limb electrodes be placed on the limbs rather than on the torso?
questions.why: Moving the limb electrodes onto the torso changes the geometry Einthoven's triangle assumes, shifting axis and amplitudes enough to create or mask ST changes. Serial tracings must also use identical placement to be comparable.

options.t: Torso placement reverses the polarity of the limb leads
options.why: Polarity is set by which cable goes where, not by proximal placement.

options.t: Torso placement shifts the axis and ST segments
The machine cannot calculate a rate from torso electrodes
options.why: Rate calculation is unaffected by limb electrode position.

options.t: Torso placement produces more muscle artifact than the limbs
options.why: Torso placement usually reduces movement artifact, which is why it is tempting.

questions.stem: A 12-lead shows a negative P wave, negative QRS and negative T in lead I, with normal precordial leads. What is the likely explanation?
questions.why: Reversing the arm leads inverts everything in lead I while the chest leads stay normal — the tell that separates it from dextrocardia, where the precordial R waves also fail to progress.

options.t: Severe left axis deviation from a hemiblock
options.why: A hemiblock shifts axis without inverting the entire complex in lead I.

options.t: The arm electrodes are reversed
A lateral wall infarct involving lead I
options.why: An infarct changes ST segments and Q waves rather than inverting every deflection.

options.t: Dextrocardia with the heart on the right
options.why: Dextrocardia would also disturb the precordial progression, which is normal here.

questions.stem: What does poor R wave progression across V1 to V6 mean?
questions.why: The R wave should grow steadily from V1 to V6. Failure to do so can mean an old anterior infarct, lead misplacement, COPD, hypertrophy or body habitus — worth noting, not diagnostic on its own.

options.t: It rules out any anterior pathology
options.why: It raises the question of anterior pathology rather than excluding it.

options.t: It is nonspecific without the clinical picture
It confirms an old anterior infarct
options.why: Old infarct is one cause among several.

options.t: It indicates lead reversal in the precordial leads
options.why: Misplacement is one possible cause, not a conclusion.

questions.stem: Which leads are considered contiguous?
questions.why: Contiguous means anatomically adjacent: II/III/aVF inferior, V1–V2 septal, V3–V4 anterior, V5–V6 with I and aVL lateral. Elevation must appear in two leads from the same group.

options.t: aVR, aVL and aVF — the three augmented leads
options.why: The augmented leads point in three different directions and are not a contiguous group.

options.t: V1, aVR and lead III
options.why: Those three look at unrelated regions.

options.t: V5, V6, I and aVL — the lateral group
II, V2 and aVL
options.why: Those span the inferior, septal and high lateral walls.

questions.stem: Match each infarct location to the artery usually responsible.
questions.why: Localizing the wall tells you the vessel, and the vessel predicts the complications — bradycardia and block with the RCA, pump failure and dysrhythmia with the LAD.
pairs: Posterior descending, usually off the RCA

questions.stem: A patient with a paced ventricular rhythm has chest pain. What limits your 12-lead interpretation?
questions.why: Ventricular pacing depolarizes the heart abnormally, producing secondary ST and T changes that look like injury. Serial tracings and the clinical picture carry more weight than the ST segments in these patients.

options.t: The 12-lead cannot be recorded while a pacemaker is firing
options.why: The tracing records normally; interpreting it is the difficulty.

options.t: Pacer spikes prevent the machine from measuring the rate
options.why: Rate measurement is unaffected by the spikes.

options.t: The pacemaker suppresses all ischemic changes completely
options.why: Changes are distorted rather than erased, and specific criteria still exist.

options.t: Paced complexes distort ST segments like an LBBB

questions.stem: Per the program's drug sheet, what aspirin dose is given for suspected cardiac chest discomfort?
questions.why: Four 81 mg chewable tablets, 324 mg total, chewed rather than swallowed for faster absorption. It is given for its antiplatelet effect, not for pain — and it is fine to give even if the patient took their daily dose already.

options.t: 650 mg — two adult tablets
options.why: That is an analgesic and antipyretic dose rather than the antiplatelet dose used here.

options.t: 162 mg — two chewable tablets
options.why: Two tablets falls short of the dose the drug sheet specifies.

options.t: 324 mg — four 81 mg chewable tablets
81 mg — one chewable tablet, the daily dose
options.why: One tablet is a daily preventive dose, not the acute antiplatelet dose.

questions.stem: Per the program's drug sheet, when is fentanyl considered for cardiac chest pain?
questions.why: The drug sheet places fentanyl after three nitroglycerin doses, or as the alternative when nitroglycerin is contraindicated — including the patient who took a PDE-5 inhibitor. Dosing is 1 mcg/kg slow push, repeatable once after five minutes.

options.t: As the first-line analgesic before any nitroglycerin
options.why: Nitroglycerin comes first because it treats the ischemia, not just the pain.

options.t: Only once a STEMI has been confirmed on the 12-lead
options.why: Its use is tied to pain control after nitroglycerin, not to a confirmed STEMI.

options.t: After three nitroglycerin doses, or if contraindicated
Instead of aspirin in patients with a bleeding history
options.why: Fentanyl is an analgesic and does nothing an antiplatelet does.

questions.stem: Why is aspirin chewed rather than swallowed whole?
questions.why: Chewing breaks the tablet up and starts absorption in the mouth and upper GI tract, inhibiting platelets minutes sooner. In an evolving occlusion those minutes are the point.

options.t: Chewing speeds absorption and platelet inhibition
Chewing prevents gastric irritation from the tablet
options.why: Chewing does not reduce the GI effects of aspirin.

options.t: Swallowing would inactivate the drug in stomach acid
options.why: Aspirin survives gastric acid; the issue is how fast it is absorbed.

options.t: Chewing allows a lower total dose to be effective
options.why: The dose is unchanged — only the speed of onset differs.

questions.stem: How does the lecture define contiguous leads?
questions.why: Contiguous means the leads look at the same part of the heart — II, III and aVF inferiorly, or I, aVL, V5 and V6 laterally — or the precordials sit next to each other, such as V3 and V4. STEMI needs more than 1 mm of elevation in two of them.

options.t: Any two leads that appear next to each other on the printout
options.why: Printout order does not reflect what the leads view.

options.t: Two leads on opposite sides of the heart
options.why: Leads on opposite sides show reciprocal change, which is the opposite relationship.

options.t: Only the three limb leads taken together
options.why: Contiguity applies across the precordial leads as well.

options.t: Two leads viewing the same aspect, or two adjacent precordials

questions.stem: Match the EKG finding to the tissue state: what does ST depression indicate?
questions.why: Three findings, three states: ST depression is ischemia, ST elevation is injury, and a pathologic Q wave is infarction. Depression is reversible; the Q wave is not.

options.t: Infarction
options.why: Infarction is marked by a pathologic Q wave.

options.t: Ischemia
Normal repolarization
options.why: Depression below the baseline is not a normal finding.

options.t: Injury
options.why: Injury shows as ST elevation.

questions.stem: What is the value of reciprocal changes, and what does their absence mean?
questions.why: Reciprocal depression, usually between the lateral and inferior leads, strongly supports a real infarct. But many confirmed infarcts show none, so its absence proves nothing.

options.t: Their presence and absence are both diagnostic
options.why: Absence is not diagnostic — plenty of real infarcts show none.

options.t: Their presence is evidence of AMI; their absence rules nothing out
They distinguish an old infarct from a new one
options.why: Age of an infarct is judged by Q waves and the clinical history.

options.t: They identify which artery is occluded
options.why: Localization comes from where the elevation is, not from the reciprocal change.

questions.stem: What are the two acceptable ways to obtain a right-sided 12-lead?
questions.why: Either move the whole precordial set across, or move V4 to the right midclavicular line at the fifth intercostal space and call it V4R. Right ventricular infarct means a preload-dependent patient — nitroglycerin is contraindicated and a low blood pressure is the presentation to expect.

options.t: Reverse the arm leads and re-record
options.why: Reversing arm leads produces an artifact, not a right-sided view.

options.t: Move all precordial leads to the right chest, or move V4 alone
Add three extra leads to the left posterior chest
options.why: Posterior leads look at the back wall, not the right ventricle.

options.t: Move all limb leads to the right side of the body
options.why: The limb leads stay where they are; the precordials are what move.

questions.stem: What terminal deflections identify a right bundle branch block?
questions.why: Look at the last part of the QRS. Terminal R in V1 and terminal S laterally is right; terminal S in V1 and terminal R laterally is left. That is what the turn-signal shortcut is actually describing.

options.t: A delta wave in V1 with a short PR
options.why: That is pre-excitation rather than a bundle branch block.

options.t: A terminal R in every lead
options.why: Bundle branch block is defined by the contrast between V1 and the lateral leads.

options.t: A terminal S in V1 with a terminal R in I, aVL and V6
options.why: That combination identifies a left bundle branch block.

options.t: A terminal R in V1 with a terminal S in I, aVL and V6

questions.stem: A young patient has an incomplete RBBB pattern with ST elevation in V1 and V2 that returns to baseline. What syndrome does this describe?
questions.why: Brugada is a sodium channel disorder: an incomplete right bundle branch block pattern with ST elevation in V1 and V2 — sometimes V3 — that comes back down to the baseline. It carries a risk of sudden death in an otherwise healthy young patient.

options.t: Brugada syndrome
Pericarditis
options.why: Pericarditis elevates diffusely with PR depression, not in V1 and V2 alone.

options.t: Early repolarization
options.why: Early repolarization is a widespread concave elevation rather than this V1-V2 pattern.

options.t: Wellens syndrome
options.why: Wellens is a T wave pattern in the anterior leads, not ST elevation with an RBBB pattern.

questions.stem: Which 12-lead findings suggest pulmonary embolism?
questions.why: S1Q3T3 — an S in lead I, a Q and inverted T in lead III — plus a new right bundle branch block and anterior ST depression. All of it reflects sudden right heart strain. The EKG supports the suspicion; it does not make the diagnosis.

options.t: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression
options.why: That pattern belongs to pericarditis.

options.t: S1Q3T3, a new right bundle branch block, ST depression in V1 to V3
Tall R waves in V1 to V3 with ST depression
options.why: Tall R with depression in those leads points at a posterior infarct.

options.t: Q3T3 with a new left bundle branch block
options.why: The bundle branch block associated with PE is right-sided.

questions.stem: Which way does the axis shift with hypertrophy, and which way with infarction?
questions.why: More muscle means a bigger vector, so the axis swings toward hypertrophied tissue. Dead tissue produces no vector at all, so the axis swings away from an infarct.

options.t: Away from the hypertrophy, toward the infarct
options.why: That reverses both relationships.

options.t: Toward the hypertrophy, away from the infarct
Away from both
options.why: Hypertrophied muscle produces a larger vector, which pulls the axis toward it.

options.t: Toward both the hypertrophy and the infarct
options.why: Dead tissue produces no vector, so the axis cannot move toward it.

questions.stem: Which two leads does the quadrant method use to determine axis?
questions.why: Lead I gives the left-right axis and aVF the up-down. Both upright is normal; I up and aVF down is left axis deviation; I down and aVF up is right; both down is extreme.

options.t: II and aVF
options.why: Lead II is used in the more detailed methods, not the quadrant shortcut.

options.t: I and aVL
options.why: Both of those look leftward, so they cannot define perpendicular quadrants.

options.t: V1 and V6
options.why: The precordials sit in the horizontal plane and are not used for this.

options.t: I and aVF

questions.stem: What finding on the 12-lead indicates right ventricular hypertrophy?
questions.why: V1 normally has a small R and a deep S because the left ventricle dominates. When the right ventricle enlarges enough for the R to exceed the S in V1, that dominance has reversed.

options.t: A deep S in V1 plus a tall R in V5
options.why: That combination is the voltage criterion for the left ventricle.

options.t: The S wave exceeds the R wave in V1
options.why: That is the normal appearance of V1.

options.t: An R wave over 11 mm in aVL
options.why: That criterion identifies left ventricular hypertrophy.

options.t: The R wave exceeds the S wave in V1

questions.stem: What are the voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy?
questions.why: Add the deepest S in V1 to the tallest R in V5 or V6; over 35 mm meets the criterion. An R over 11 mm in aVL is the other accepted measurement, and either one can stand alone.

options.t: S in V1 plus R in V5 or V6 over 35 mm, or R in aVL over 11 mm
Any QRS wider than 0.12 seconds in two contiguous leads
options.why: A wide QRS is a conduction finding, not a voltage criterion.

options.t: S in V1 plus R in V5 or V6 over 20 mm, or R in aVL over 5 mm
options.why: Both thresholds are below the values taught.

options.t: R exceeding S in V1, with no measurement of the lateral leads
options.why: That criterion identifies right ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: Check the R wave progression across the chest leads on this tracing. What does it show?
questions.why: The R grows and the S shrinks moving from V1 across to V6, with the transition — where R and S are about equal — usually falling at V3 or V4. Failure to progress raises the question of an old anterior infarct, lead misplacement, COPD or body habitus.

options.t: Reversed progression, with the tallest R in V1
options.why: V1 shows a small r with a deep S; the tall R waves are laterally.

options.t: A transition that fails to appear across the precordial leads
options.why: The transition is visible between V3 and V4.

options.t: Poor R wave progression, suggesting an old anterior infarct
options.why: The R wave grows steadily here, which is exactly what poor progression lacks.

options.t: Normal progression, from an rS in V1 to a dominant R by V5

questions.stem: Why is the whole complex negative in aVR on a normal tracing?
questions.why: Normal depolarization runs down and to the left. aVR sits up and to the right, so the wave moves away from it — P, QRS and T all point down. An upright complex in aVR usually means the limb leads are reversed.

options.t: The aVR electrode is placed in reverse polarity by design
options.why: Polarity is not inverted; the lead's viewing angle is simply opposite.

options.t: The right arm is further from the heart than the left
options.why: Distance changes amplitude, not the direction of the deflection.

options.t: aVR records only atrial activity, which is small and negative
options.why: aVR records the same ventricular depolarization every other lead does.

options.t: aVR looks at the heart from the opposite direction to depolarization

questions.stem: Which leads carry the ST elevation on this tracing, and what does that locate?
questions.why: Elevation across the mid-precordial leads points at the anterior wall and the left anterior descending artery — which supplies a large share of the left ventricle. Anterior infarcts carry the highest risk of pump failure.

options.t: II, III and aVF — the inferior wall, RCA territory
options.why: Those leads show depression here, not elevation.

options.t: V1 and V2 alone — the septum in isolation
options.why: The elevation extends beyond the septal leads into V3 and V4.

options.t: V5, V6, I and aVL — the lateral wall
options.why: The lateral leads are comparatively unremarkable on this tracing.

options.t: V2 through V4 — the anterior wall, LAD territory

questions.stem: Look at II, III and aVF on this anterior tracing. What are those leads showing?
questions.why: Leads facing away from the injured wall see the same injury current heading away from them, so the ST segment dips. Its presence makes the elevation far more likely to be a genuine occlusion.

options.t: Normal ST segments with no abnormality
options.why: The segments sit below the baseline in those leads.

options.t: A second, inferior infarct occurring at the same time
options.why: Reciprocal change is one injury viewed from the other side, not a second infarct.

options.t: Reciprocal ST depression
Digitalis effect on the ST segments
options.why: Digitalis produces a scooped depression across many leads, unrelated to a territorial pattern.

questions.stem: Identify the infarct territory on this tracing and name the artery usually responsible.
questions.why: Elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL is the inferior pattern, and in most people that wall belongs to the right coronary artery — which is why these patients so often arrive bradycardic.

options.t: Lateral wall — the circumflex
options.why: I and aVL show depression rather than elevation.

options.t: Inferior wall — the right coronary artery
Anterior wall — the left anterior descending
options.why: The precordial leads are comparatively unremarkable here.

options.t: Septum — the septal branches of the LAD
options.why: V1 and V2 do not carry the elevation on this tracing.

questions.stem: Given this tracing, what is your next 12-lead step, and how does it change management?
questions.why: The RCA supplies the right ventricle proximally, so an inferior STEMI raises that question every time. If V4R is elevated, that ventricle is preload-dependent and nitroglycerin can drop the pressure sharply.

options.t: Get V7 through V9 — posterior involvement changes the destination
options.why: Posterior leads are worth adding when V1–V3 show depression, and they would not change the destination.

options.t: Nothing further — the diagnosis is already complete
options.why: An inferior STEMI is not fully characterized until the right ventricle has been checked.

options.t: Repeat the same 12-lead to confirm the elevation is real
options.why: Three contiguous leads already carry it; a repeat adds nothing new.

options.t: Get V4R — right ventricular involvement changes nitroglycerin use

questions.stem: This inferior STEMI patient has a heart rate in the 50s. Why is that expected?
questions.why: The RCA supplies the SA node in about 60% of people and the AV node in roughly 90%. Lose flow through it and the pacemaker and the junction both suffer — bradycardia and heart block travel with inferior infarcts.

options.t: Pain and anxiety typically slow the rate in an infarct
options.why: Pain and anxiety usually raise the rate.

options.t: The RCA also feeds the SA and AV nodes
Reduced stroke volume triggers a reflex bradycardia
options.why: A falling stroke volume normally produces a compensatory tachycardia.

options.t: Inferior infarcts damage the bundle branches directly
options.why: The bundle branches are usually supplied by the left system.

questions.stem: Which wall is infarcting on this tracing?
questions.why: Elevation in the high lateral pair (I and aVL) together with the low lateral pair (V5 and V6), with reciprocal depression inferiorly, is the lateral pattern — usually the circumflex.

options.t: The inferior wall — II, III and aVF
options.why: Those leads carry the reciprocal depression here, not the elevation.

options.t: The lateral wall — I, aVL, V5 and V6
The posterior wall — V1 through V3 in mirror image
options.why: There are no tall R waves with depression in the septal leads.

options.t: The anterior wall — V3 and V4
options.why: The mid-precordial leads are relatively unremarkable.

questions.stem: V1 through V3 on this tracing show ST depression with unusually tall R waves. What does that mean?
questions.why: No standard lead looks at the back of the heart, so a posterior infarct shows up reversed in the septal leads: depression instead of elevation, tall R waves instead of Q waves. V7 through V9 confirm it.

options.t: A posterior infarct, seen in mirror image
Right ventricular hypertrophy
options.why: Hypertrophy would not produce ST depression in this pattern.

options.t: Normal septal forces in a thin-chested patient
options.why: A normal V1 shows a small r with a deep S, not a dominant R.

options.t: Anterior ischemia without infarction
options.why: Ischemia alone would not build the tall R waves seen here.

questions.stem: This tracing shows ST elevation in almost every lead. What does that pattern indicate?
questions.why: Pericarditis inflames the entire pericardium, so the elevation is diffuse rather than territorial, concave upward, and accompanied by PR depression — with no reciprocal changes, which is the key separator from a STEMI.

options.t: A massive infarct involving several coronary territories
options.why: An occlusion follows one vessel's territory; it does not elevate every lead at once.

options.t: Early repolarization in a young athletic patient
options.why: Early repolarization is usually confined to the precordial leads and lacks PR depression.

options.t: Pericarditis — inflammation of the whole sac
Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain
options.why: Hypertrophy produces high voltage with lateral strain, not diffuse elevation.

questions.stem: Beyond the diffuse elevation, which finding on this tracing supports pericarditis over a STEMI?
questions.why: PR depression comes from atrial involvement in the inflammation and is characteristic. Just as telling is what is missing: a real occlusion produces reciprocal depression somewhere, and pericarditis does not.

options.t: Q waves developing in the inferior leads
options.why: Q waves mark established necrosis, which points to infarction.

options.t: PR segment depression, with no reciprocal changes anywhere
A widened QRS across the precordial leads
options.why: QRS widening reflects a conduction problem rather than pericardial inflammation.

options.t: ST depression in the leads opposite the elevation
options.why: Reciprocal depression argues for an occlusion, not pericarditis.

questions.stem: The QRS on this tracing is wider than 0.12. Look at V1 — which block is it?
questions.why: With a wide QRS, look at V1: a terminal upward deflection is a right bundle branch block, a broad downward one is a left. Up is right, down is left — the turn-signal rule.

options.t: A ventricular escape rhythm rather than a block
options.why: P waves precede each complex, so the impulse is coming from above.

options.t: Right bundle branch block, from the terminal upward deflection
options.why: A terminal upward deflection in V1 is the right-sided pattern; this one points down.

options.t: Left bundle branch block, from the broad downward V1 complex
An accelerated idioventricular rhythm
options.why: AIVR has no P waves, and this tracing has them.

questions.stem: A patient with chest pain has this tracing, and it is new since their last ECG. How should it be treated?
questions.why: A left bundle branch block distorts ST segments on its own, so ordinary STEMI criteria stop working. A new one with ischemic symptoms is treated as a STEMI equivalent — which is why knowing it is new matters so much.

options.t: As a STEMI equivalent — activate the cath lab
As a stable conduction problem needing no urgent action
options.why: A new one in a patient with ischemic symptoms is not a benign finding.

options.t: As a contraindication to aspirin and nitroglycerin
options.why: Neither drug is contraindicated by a conduction block.

options.t: As an indication for immediate transcutaneous pacing
options.why: A bundle branch block with a stable rate does not call for pacing.

questions.stem: Look at the terminal deflection in V1 on this wide-complex tracing. Which block is present?
questions.why: The right ventricle depolarizes late, producing the terminal R' in V1 — the rabbit ears — with a wide slurred S in I and V6. A right bundle branch block is far more often benign than a left.

options.t: Left bundle branch block
options.why: A left block gives a broad downward complex in V1, not a terminal upward one.

options.t: A left anterior fascicular block
options.why: A fascicular block shifts the axis without widening the QRS this far.

options.t: Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation
options.why: Pre-excitation shows a short PR with a delta wave slurring into the QRS.

options.t: Right bundle branch block

questions.stem: The T waves on this tracing are tall, narrow and peaked in nearly every lead. What should you suspect?
questions.why: Rising potassium peaks the T waves first, then flattens the P waves and widens the QRS toward a sine wave. In a dialysis patient or a crush injury this is one of the most treatable causes of an arrest.

options.t: Normal variant T waves in a young patient
options.why: Peaked T waves in every lead with a widened QRS is not a normal variant.

options.t: Hyperkalemia
Hyperacute T waves of a very early STEMI
options.why: Hyperacute T waves are confined to one territory; these are everywhere.

options.t: Hypokalemia with prominent U waves
options.why: Low potassium flattens the T wave and adds a U wave after it.

questions.stem: This patient missed dialysis and has this tracing. What does the widening QRS tell you about urgency?
questions.why: Peaked T waves are the early warning; a widening QRS means conduction itself is failing, and the next steps on that path are a sine wave and arrest. That patient needs transport and treatment now.

options.t: The potassium is high enough to threaten the rhythm
Widening indicates the potassium is beginning to fall
options.why: Widening marks worsening, not resolution.

options.t: The widening is unrelated to potassium and can be ignored
options.why: QRS widening is a recognized hyperkalemia progression, not an incidental finding.

options.t: The patient has developed a bundle branch block
options.why: A block widens the QRS with a characteristic V1 shape, absent here.

questions.stem: This tracing shows deep S waves in V1 and V2 with tall R waves in V5 and V6. What does that suggest?
questions.why: A thickened left ventricle generates more voltage, so the leads facing it record tall R waves and the leads opposite record deep S waves. The associated ST depression and T inversion laterally is the strain pattern — not ischemia, though it can look like it.

options.t: A posterior infarct in mirror image
options.why: A posterior pattern shows tall R waves in V1 with depression, not deep S waves.

options.t: Right ventricular hypertrophy
options.why: Right-sided hypertrophy produces a tall R in V1 rather than a deep S.

options.t: Left ventricular hypertrophy
An anterolateral STEMI
options.why: Voltage alone is not injury; there is no territorial ST elevation here.

questions.stem: Before reading any 12-lead for ischemia, what should you confirm about the tracing itself?
questions.why: Half standardization halves every amplitude. Limb leads on the torso shift the axis. A wandering baseline makes ST measurement guesswork. Check the recording before you trust anything you read off it.

options.t: Standard calibration, correct lead placement, and a clean baseline
That the patient's blood pressure was taken in both arms
options.why: Worth doing for a suspected dissection, but it says nothing about the tracing.

options.t: That the machine's own interpretation agrees with yours
options.why: The machine's read is a prompt, not a verification of the recording.

options.t: That the strip is at least ten seconds long
options.why: Length does not validate calibration or placement.
